title: Multiton Pattern
oneLiner: Guarantees exactly one instance per key, backed by a registry — Singleton's guarantee, multiplied across a lookup table.

hero.name: The Registrar
hero.catchphrase: Not one instance — one instance PER KEY, and I keep the ledger.
hero.power: Maintains one guaranteed instance per key, so the same key always resolves to the exact same object.
hero.weakness: It's Singleton's hidden-dependency problem, multiplied by every key — a global registry in disguise, with all the same testability headaches.
hero.origin: The Registrar appeared after a multi-region app's logger was accidentally instantiated twice for the same 'us-east' region, causing two separate log buffers to silently split what should've been one stream.

story.problem: A regional logger is constructed wherever it's needed: `new RegionLogger("us-east")` appears in three different files. Each call creates a separate instance for the same region, splitting what should be one unified log stream.
story.solution: The Registrar keeps a map from region key to logger instance. `RegionLogger.getInstance("us-east")` always returns the exact same object for that key, creating it only the first time.
story.result: Every part of the app sharing a region key now shares the exact same logger instance. Logs for 'us-east' are finally unified into one stream.

before: Same key constructs a new instance every time
State for the same logical key gets split across instances
No single source of truth per key
after: Same key always resolves to the exact same instance
State for a given key stays unified, no matter who asks
One registry is the single source of truth per key

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Two log buffers exist for 'us-east', each missing half the entries the other one has.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: We have two separate RegionLogger instances for the same region! No wonder the log stream looks incomplete.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Registrar appears holding a ledger, one row per region key, each pointing to exactly one logger.
panels.speaker: The Registrar
panels.dialogue: Stop constructing a new logger every time. Ask ME for the 'us-east' logger — I'll hand you the same one, every time.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: getInstance('us-east') checks the registry map. If it exists, return it. If not, create it once and register it.
panels.speaker: The Registrar
panels.dialogue: Ask for the same key twice, get the same object twice. The registry guarantees it, no matter who's asking or when.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: One unified log stream per region, no matter how many files ask for it.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One logger per region now, guaranteed. The log stream is finally complete and unified.

useWhen: You need Singleton's 'exactly one instance' guarantee, but scoped per key rather than globally (per tenant, per region, per connection type).
The set of valid keys is well-understood and the number of instances stays reasonable.
Multiple parts of the app need to share the exact same instance for a given key without explicitly passing it around.
avoidWhen: A single global instance (plain Singleton) or explicit dependency injection would work just as well.
The set of keys is unbounded or attacker-controlled, risking unbounded memory growth in the registry.
You're using it as a shortcut to avoid proper dependency injection — it hides coupling exactly like Singleton does.
commonMistakes: Letting the registry grow unbounded with dynamic or untrusted keys, silently leaking memory over time.
Using Multiton where a simple parameterized constructor plus normal dependency injection would be clearer and more testable.
Forgetting that Multiton inherits every one of Singleton's testing and hidden-coupling problems, just multiplied across keys.
Not thread-safing the registry's get-or-create logic, risking two instances being created for the same key under concurrency.
explanation.realWorldExample: Per-tenant service instances in multi-tenant SaaS apps, per-database-connection-type client caches, and per-region configuration objects are common real-world Multiton use cases.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: So you're just... Singleton, but with a map instead of one variable?

conversation.speaker: The Registrar
conversation.message: That's exactly it. Same guarantee — exactly one instance — just keyed instead of singular. And I inherit Singleton's exact same weakness: hidden global state, just spread across more keys.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When should I reach for plain dependency injection instead?

conversation.speaker: The Registrar
conversation.message: Almost always, honestly. If you can pass the right instance to whoever needs it explicitly, do that. I'm for cases where a global, key-based lookup genuinely can't be avoided.

codeBattle.scenario: Your multi-region app needs exactly one metrics collector per AWS region, shared across every service in that region, with no duplicate collectors ever created for the same region.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Registrar guarantees exactly one metrics collector per region key, unlike Singleton (only one instance total) or Object Pool (many interchangeable instances).

quiz.question: How does Multiton differ from Singleton?
options: Multiton guarantees one instance per key, via a registry; Singleton guarantees exactly one instance total
They are identical patterns under different names
Multiton allows unlimited instances per key; Singleton allows none
Singleton requires a database; Multiton does not
quiz.answer: Multiton guarantees one instance per key, via a registry; Singleton guarantees exactly one instance total
quiz.explanation: Multiton generalizes Singleton's guarantee across a set of keys instead of a single global instance.

quiz.question: What internal structure does Multiton typically use to enforce its guarantee?
options: A map/registry from key to instance
A linked list of all created objects
A database table that's queried on every access
quiz.answer: A map/registry from key to instance
quiz.explanation: The registry is what lets Multiton check 'does this key already have an instance?' before creating a new one.

quiz.question: What weakness does Multiton inherit directly from Singleton?
options: Hidden global state that complicates testing and creates implicit coupling
The inability to ever have more than one instance
quiz.answer: Hidden global state that complicates testing and creates implicit coupling
quiz.explanation: Multiton is still a global, static registry — just keyed — so it carries Singleton's classic downsides, multiplied across keys.

quiz.question: What's a risk specific to Multiton (beyond plain Singleton)?
options: An unbounded or attacker-controlled set of keys can cause the registry to grow without limit
It can only ever store one key at a time
It cannot be used in TypeScript
quiz.answer: An unbounded or attacker-controlled set of keys can cause the registry to grow without limit
quiz.explanation: Because Multiton keeps one instance per distinct key, an uncontrolled key space can lead to unbounded memory growth.
